newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algerians, seeking peace, vote in general election.
newsitem.headline: Algerians, seeking peace, vote in general election.

text.p: Millions of Algerians turned out in bright sunshine on Thursday to vote in their first parliamentary election in more than five years of violence and bloodshed -- blamed by officials on Moslem fundamentalists.

Many said they were seeking peace through the ballot box. Even as they voted, an Islam-oriented party contesting the poll said a bomb had seriously wounded two local election observers in a car near Djelfa in central Algiers.
Voting started slowly but by 11 a.m. (1000 GMT) 17.51 percent, or around three million of the near-17 million electorate, had cast their ballots, including President Liamine Zeroual.
Algeria's state radio said this compared with 22.05 percent turnout in a 1995 presidential poll.
In the capital, where bombs early this week ripped through buses and a crowded market, men and women clutching electoral cards told Reuters they were voting for an end to the strife.

"I voted for peace for me and my children," Ahmed Yanaguen, 58, told Reuters. Yanaguen and his wife, wearing a black veil, were the first to vote at El-Warda school in the capital's Telemly neighbourhood. The deputy head of the El-Warda station said voting was slow but he expected it to pick up.

Armed plainclothes police guarded polling stations, most of which opened at 8 a.m. (0700 GMT). Troops and police, backed by armoured troop carriers, deployed at entrances to Algiers and in city streets where Moslem rebels have carried out attacks.
The Tribune newspaper said the nation's 16.8 million voters were choosing "an Assembly of hope".

Zeroual cast his vote early in Ghazali school polling station in Algeria's Mouradia district. He told reporters he was "convinced that the Algerian people will seize this historic opportunity and vote in large numbers."

His government says the poll is a key step towards ending civil strife that began shortly after the army-backed authorities in January 1992 cancelled elections that the radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) was poised to win.
About 60,000 people have died in the conflict.

The FIS is outlawed, but one man near a city voting station said: "Despite what they say, that the FIS has disappeared, I am not going to vote because I don't want to go back on my religious and political principles."
And in the fundamentalist strongholds of Bab El-Oued and the Casbah in the capital, eyewitnesses reported polling stations practically empty except for a few elderly people.
Voters are casting ballots to elect a 380-member National Assembly (lower house) from more than 7,000 candidates standing for 39 political parties.

The new parliament will be Algeria's first elected multi-party assembly since independence in 1962. For nearly 30 years until the first attempt at a democratic parliamentary vote in December 1991, the oil and gas producing country was run as a one-party state by the National Liberation Front (FLN).
In some parts of the vast North African country, such as the eastern town of Annaba, local reporters said queues had started to form well before the voting stations opened.

It was in Annaba in June 1992 that President Mohamed Boudiaf was assassinated after only six months in power in the early days of violence. The latest attacks -- bombs in Algiers -- in three days to last Monday killed 22 people and wounded about 120.
More than 37,500 polling stations will remain open until 7 p.m. (1800 GMT) although local authorities may extend polling hours in some centres to help voters.
Frontrunners are the National Democratic Rally (RND), which groups Zeroual supporters, and the Islam-oriented Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS) of moderate Islamist leader Mahfoud Nahnah.
Other leading parties include the Socialist Forces Front (FFS) of secularist opposition leader Hocine Ait Ahmed and the Rally for Culture and Democracy of anti-Islamist Said Saadi.
A new proportional representation law virtually guarantees that at least four or five parties will be in parliament with little chance of a single party holding an absolute majority.
Because of the new system, officials are reluctant to forecast when final results will be available. Newspapers say they should be out sometime on Friday.
